walkthroughs.h2: How greenhouse gases warm the Earth
walkthroughs.body_html: Shortwave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the surface. Outgoing longwave radiation is partly absorbed by GHGs and re-emitted in all directions, including back to the surface. CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour and halocarbons contribute, with positive feedbacks from water vapour and ice albedo amplifying the effect.

Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from ~280 ppm pre-industrial to about 420 ppm in the 2020s. Global mean surface temperature is now about 1.1-1.2 °C above pre-industrial levels. Sea-surface temperatures, ocean heat content and glacier mass balance all show consistent trends.

The IPCC AR6 Working Group I report estimates a remaining carbon budget of roughly 500 GtCO₂ for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5 °C. At current emissions of around 40 GtCO₂/yr, this budget would be exhausted in roughly a decade, illustrating the urgency of rapid mitigation.

mcqs.q: What does a 'large scale' map mean?
options: A large-scale map covers a small area in high detail (e.g. 1:25,000 OS map of one town); a small-scale map covers a large area in less detail (e.g. 1:1,000,000 world atlas).
Large scale means the map is physically big.
It is the hole in the ozone layer letting in more sun.
A large-scale map shows a large area.

mcqs.q: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: The strengthening of the natural greenhouse effect by human activities (mainly burning fossil fuels) which add CO2 and other gases to the atmosphere.
It is the hole in the ozone layer letting in more sun.
Biotic and abiotic both refer to types of soil.
The greenhouse effect is entirely man-made and harmful.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem?
options: Biotic and abiotic both refer to types of soil.
Biotic means animals and abiotic means plants.
Large scale means the map is physically big.
Biotic components are all living organisms (plants, animals, microbes); abiotic components are non-living factors (climate, soil, water, light, rock).
